newsitem.title: FRANCE: One-day strikes hit France in echo of 1995 unrest.
newsitem.headline: One-day strikes hit France in echo of 1995 unrest.

text.p: Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through cities across France on Thursday as a 24-hour public employees' strike against government cuts and record unemployment hit rail, air, school and postal services.

Many schools closed, domestic and short-haul flights were drastically reduced and only one train in three was running as a result of the first major labour protest since a crippling public sector strike lasting nearly four weeks in late 1995.
As the day drew to a close, a key trade union leader urged unions to join in a new day of nationwide protests next month.
"We now have the momentum going, which will continue and grow stronger each day," Louis Viannet, secretary general of the Communist-led CGT union, told RTL radio.
"To build on the momentum created on this day of October 17, we urge all labour organisations to join with us in a new major initiative on around November 15."
About half of France's teachers stayed away from work, as did about a third of civil servants and postal and France Telecom staff, unions and the government said.
Separately, many doctors refused to treat the sick in a protest over health care reforms.
But the Paris bus and Metro network was operating close to normal, giving the impression of a city still ticking along, in contrast to the chaos of last year's 24-day transport strike.

"All together in defence of public service, jobs and purchasing power," read the banner at the head of a giant march that sprawled through central Paris. The CGT said 100,000 people took part but police put the number at about 23,000.

The strike was sparked by fears among five million public employees of job cuts under Prime Minister Alain Juppe's austerity drive to cut France's deficit in time for the planned single European Union currency in 1999.

An opinion poll for the daily Le Parisien newspaper said 64 percent of people sympathised with the strike. Protesters in Bordeaux, the southwestern city where Juppe serves as mayor, burned the prime minister in effigy.
Despite the big turnout, the Paris march highlighted old divisions in the labour movement over the social security reform which was one of the catalysts for last year's strike.
CGT marchers hurled abuse at Nicole Notat, whose CFDT union joined the stoppage though it backed Juppe's welfare reform plans and stayed out of last year's strikes.
Notat struck back, complaining that it was "unpleasant and incongruous that this strike is gradually becoming a catch-all."

She also carped to RTL radio that the doctors' strike was diverting the protest from its focus on the public sector and accused Viannet of constantly complaining while failing to offer realistic alternatives.
Union leaders differed over whether the strike presaged a repeat of the wave of labour unrest last November and December.
"There is growing anger at the grassroots which will be expressed more and more strongly because people are fed up," Viannet insisted on Europe 1 radio.

Civil servants were protesting against government plans to trim their numbers by 6,000 next year. Teachers will bear the brunt of the austerity drive, with a loss of 2,300 permanent jobs and the layoff of around 15,000 short-term contract staff.

The strikes and demonstrations reflected widespread disenchantment with conservative President Jacques Chirac, who was elected in May 1995 after promising to make unemployment his top priority, to cut taxes and to allow higher wages.

Unemployment has since reached a record 12.6 percent and is still rising, taxes have gone up and purchasing power has stagnated after Chirac changed his tune a year ago, saying that cutting the deficit was France's top priority.
